introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Pure Mathematics with Mechanics, Paper 3 (0765/3), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Time allowed: three hours.**

Full marks may be obtained for answers to ALL questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Mathematical formulae booklets published by the Board are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. Start each question on a fresh page.
enonce_intro_markdown:
A particle is projected from a point $O$ on a horizontal plane with speed $u$ at an angle $\alpha$ to the plane. The particle just clears two vertical walls, each of height $h$, at horizontal distances $2h$ and $4h$ from $O$.

Show that
incertitudes: Question 3 (b) : le sujet imprime « 2u^2 = 12h », qui est faux. Les deux murs (hauteur h, abscisses 2h et 4h) donnent tan(alpha) = 3/4 et u^2 = 125h/2, soit 2u^2 = 125h ; seule cette valeur redonne H = 9h/8 en (c) (avec 12h on obtiendrait H = 27h/250 < h). Le corrigé démontre 2u^2 = 125h et signale que « 12h » est une coquille (le chiffre 5 perdu). Le sujet imprime « Take g as 10 m s^-2 » : valeur retenue g = 10.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model.** Take $O$ as origin, $x$ horizontal in the direction of projection and $y$ vertically upwards (positive upwards, so the acceleration is $-g$). The particle moves as a projectile under gravity only, with $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

$$x = (u\cos\alpha)\,t,\qquad y = (u\sin\alpha)\,t - \tfrac12 g t^2$$

Eliminating $t$ gives the equation of the trajectory:

$$y = x\tan\alpha - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\alpha} = x\tan\alpha - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2}\left(1 + \tan^2\alpha\right)$$

Write $T = \tan\alpha$ and $k = \dfrac{g(1 + T^2)}{2u^2}$ (a constant), so that $y = Tx - kx^2$.

"Just clears a wall" means that the trajectory passes through the top of the wall, so $y = h$ at $x = 2h$ and at $x = 4h$.

At $x = 2h$: $\ h = 2hT - 4h^2k \;\Rightarrow\; 1 = 2T - 4hk \qquad (1)$

At $x = 4h$: $\ h = 4hT - 16h^2k \;\Rightarrow\; 1 = 4T - 16hk \qquad (2)$

Let $p = hk$. Then $(2) - 2\times(1)$ gives $1 - 2 = -16p + 8p$, so $p = \dfrac18$, that is $hk = \dfrac18$ $\qquad (3)$.

Substituting into (1): $2T = 1 + 4p = 1 + \dfrac12 = \dfrac32$, so $T = \dfrac34$.

(Check in (2): $4\cdot\dfrac34 - 16\cdot\dfrac18 = 3 - 2 = 1$.)

$$\tan\alpha = \frac34 \;\Rightarrow\; 4\tan\alpha = 3.\qquad\blacksquare$$

**The printed result is a misprint.** The correct result, which the data force, is $2u^2 = 125h$ (the digit $5$ has been lost in the printed "$12h$"). It is shown below, and part (c) cannot hold with $12h$.

From part (a), $\tan\alpha = \dfrac34$ and $hk = \dfrac18$, where $k = \dfrac{g(1 + \tan^2\alpha)}{2u^2}$ and $g = 10$.

$$1 + \tan^2\alpha = 1 + \frac{9}{16} = \frac{25}{16}\;\Rightarrow\; k = \frac{10\cdot\frac{25}{16}}{2u^2} = \frac{125}{16\,u^2}$$

$$hk = \frac18 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{125\,h}{16\,u^2} = \frac18 \;\Rightarrow\; u^2 = \frac{125 \cdot 8\,h}{16} = \frac{125}{2}\,h \;\Rightarrow\; 2u^2 = 125h$$

**Why $12h$ is impossible.** If $2u^2 = 12h$ then $u^2 = 6h$ and the maximum height would be $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g} = \dfrac{6h\cdot\frac{9}{25}}{20} = \dfrac{27}{250}h$, which is less than $h$: the particle could never reach the top of the walls, and it contradicts part (c), $H = \dfrac98 h$.

**Hence $2u^2 = 125h$** (the value printed, "$12h$", is a misprint of this).

At the highest point the vertical component of velocity is zero. Using $v_y^2 = (u\sin\alpha)^2 - 2gH = 0$:

$$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}$$

From part (a), $\tan\alpha = \dfrac34$, so $\sin^2\alpha = \dfrac{\tan^2\alpha}{1 + \tan^2\alpha} = \dfrac{9/16}{25/16} = \dfrac{9}{25}$. From part (b), $u^2 = \dfrac{125}{2}h$. With $g = 10$:

$$H = \frac{\frac{125}{2}h\cdot\frac{9}{25}}{2\times 10} = \frac{\frac{45}{2}h}{20} = \frac{45}{40}h = \frac98\,h.\qquad\blacksquare$$

(Check with the trajectory: the highest point is at $x = \dfrac{T}{2k} = \dfrac{3/4}{2/(8h)} = 3h$, between the two walls, and $y = T x - kx^2 = \dfrac94 h - \dfrac{9h^2}{8h} = \dfrac98 h$.)
